learn.title: Green Hydrogen: PEM vs Alkaline Electrolysis
learn.intro: Green hydrogen produced via water electrolysis using renewable electricity is key to decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors like steel, chemicals, and shipping. Choosing between Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) and alkaline electrolyzers affects efficiency, cost, and scalability. Understanding these technologies helps policymakers and investors make informed decisions about future energy infrastructure.
learn.c1_title: ⚡ PEM Electrolyzers: Fast Response, High Efficiency
learn.c1_text: PEM electrolyzers use a solid polymer membrane and operate at high current densities, making them ideal for variable renewable sources like solar and wind. They respond quickly to power fluctuations and require less water purification. Think of PEM as a sports car—agile and efficient but more expensive upfront compared to traditional systems.
learn.c2_title: 🏭 Alkaline Electrolyzers: Mature Tech, Lower Cost
learn.c2_text: Alkaline electrolyzers use liquid potassium hydroxide and have been commercially deployed for decades. They’re cheaper per kW but slower to respond to load changes. Imagine them as reliable trucks—less nimble but cost-effective for large-scale, steady operations in industrial settings.
learn.c3_title: 🇮🇳 India’s Green Hydrogen Mission: Scaling Up
learn.c3_text: India aims to become a global hub for green hydrogen manufacturing under its National Green Hydrogen Mission. The government plans to set up 5 MMTA (million metric tonnes per annum) production capacity by 2030. Pilot projects by IOCL and NTPC are testing both PEM and alkaline systems to determine optimal deployment strategies.
learn.stat1: Global green hydrogen demand could reach 150 TWh by 2030 (IRENA)
learn.stat2: PEM electrolyzers achieve up to 80% efficiency vs 70% for alkaline systems

learn.title: Hydrogen Colours: Blue, Green, and Grey Explained
learn.intro: Not all hydrogen is created equal. Its environmental impact depends on how it's produced. Grey comes from fossil fuels without carbon capture, blue adds carbon capture, and green uses renewables. Understanding these distinctions is crucial for evaluating hydrogen projects' true climate benefits and guiding sustainable investment choices.
learn.c1_text: Grey hydrogen is made by steam methane reforming natural gas without capturing CO2 emissions. It accounts for over 95% of global hydrogen production today. While cheapest initially, it emits 9–12 kg of CO2 per kg of hydrogen—equivalent to burning heavy fuel oil. This makes it a major emitter in chemical industries.
learn.c2_title: 🔵 Blue Hydrogen: Fossil Fuel with Carbon Capture
learn.c2_text: Blue hydrogen also starts with natural gas but includes carbon capture and storage (CCS) to trap most CO2 emissions. If CCS captures 90%, blue H2 can reduce emissions by up to 80%. However, methane leaks during production may offset some benefits, sparking debate over its long-term viability.
learn.c3_title: 🇮🇳 India’s Focus on Green Over Blue Hydrogen
learn.c3_text: India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission prioritizes green hydrogen due to abundant solar and wind resources. Unlike countries relying on blue due to existing gas infrastructure, India skips blue to avoid fossil fuel lock-in. Plans include 5000 MW renewable capacity dedicated to green hydrogen production by 2030.

learn.stat3: Green hydrogen currently costs $3–8/kg vs $1–2/kg for grey (2024)

learn.title: Capacity Factor: Why Rated Power ≠ Actual Output
learn.intro: A wind turbine rated at 5 MW doesn’t always produce 5 MW. Capacity factor measures actual output versus maximum possible output over time. It explains why renewables vary and why grids need flexibility. Grasping this concept helps understand energy planning, pricing, and reliability challenges in transitioning power systems.
learn.c1_text: Capacity factor = actual energy produced ÷ maximum possible energy if running at full power continuously. For example, a 100 MW solar farm producing 250,000 MWh/year has a 28.5% capacity factor (250,000 ÷ [100×8760]). It reflects real-world availability and resource quality—not just equipment size.
learn.c2_title: 🌬️ Wind vs Solar: Different Patterns, Same Metric
learn.c2_text: Onshore wind typically achieves 35–45% capacity factors, offshore up to 50%. Utility-scale solar ranges from 20–30%, rooftop lower due to shading. These numbers help compare technologies fairly and explain why diversified portfolios stabilize supply. Higher capacity factors mean more predictable, consistent clean energy delivery.
learn.c3_text: India’s average solar plant operates at ~22% capacity factor, while wind farms hit ~25%. However, newer sites in Rajasthan and Gujarat report higher yields thanks to better irradiance mapping and turbine placement. The government targets raising overall renewable capacity factors through hybrid projects combining solar and storage.

learn.title: Pumped Hydro Storage: Nature’s Giant Battery
learn.intro: Pumped hydro storage (PHS) stores excess electricity by pumping water uphill, then releases it through turbines when needed. Making up over 90% of global energy storage, PHS balances supply and demand across days or seasons. As variable renewables grow, PHS remains essential for grid stability and long-duration backup power.
learn.c1_text: During low-demand periods, surplus electricity pumps water from a lower reservoir to an upper one. When demand peaks, water flows down through turbines generating power. A typical plant like Bath County in Virginia can store 24 GWh—enough to power 600,000 homes for a day. Efficiency ranges from 70–85%.
learn.c2_text: Unlike lithium-ion batteries that discharge in hours, PHS provides multi-day or seasonal storage. It stabilizes frequency, prevents blackouts, and defers transmission upgrades. With response times under 15 minutes, PHS reacts faster than coal or nuclear plants—making it invaluable for managing sudden spikes or drops in renewable generation.
learn.c3_text: India plans to add 96 GW of pumped hydro storage by 2030 to support its 500 GW non-fossil target. Key projects include the 3 GW Koel-Karo plant in Jharkhand and 6 GW in Himachal Pradesh. These will provide critical peaking power and integrate more solar/wind into the national grid efficiently.

learn.title: India’s EV Policy: PM e-DRIVE and State Schemes
learn.intro: India’s electric vehicle adoption hinges on central and state policies working together. The Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid and Electric Vehicles (FAME) scheme, now in Phase II, supports buyer incentives and charging infrastructure. Complemented by state-level EV policies, these frameworks aim to boost domestic manufacturing and accelerate fleet electrification.
learn.c1_text: Launched in 2015, FAME Phase II allocates ₹10,000 crore (~$1.2 billion) until 2024 to subsidize EV purchases and build charging stations. So far, over 1.1 million EVs have received incentives. Priority segments include two-wheelers, three-wheelers, and buses. The scheme also funds public charging points along highways and cities.
learn.c2_text: States like Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, and Karnataka offer additional subsidies, tax breaks, and registration waivers. Some mandate fleet electrification for taxis and public transport. Together with central support, these policies create a favorable ecosystem for automakers and consumers, pushing sales beyond urban elites toward mass-market adoption.
learn.c3_text: Under the India EV Mission, the goal is 30% private vehicle sales electric by 2030. To meet this, over 26 states have notified EV policies. NITI Aayog estimates India needs 1.9 million charging points by 2030. Investments in lithium-ion cell plants and battery swapping networks are rising fast, especially in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.

learn.title: Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G): EVs Power the Grid
learn.intro: Electric vehicles aren’t just consumers—they can become mobile energy assets. Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) lets EVs discharge stored battery power back to the grid during peak demand. This two-way flow enhances grid resilience, integrates more renewables, and even earns drivers revenue. As EV numbers surge, V2G unlocks massive flexible capacity for smart grids.
learn.c1_text: V2G-equipped EVs use bidirectional chargers to send power from their batteries to homes or the grid. Most modern EVs can supply 3–10 kW temporarily. During blackouts, they act as backup generators. In normal operation, aggregators pool fleets to sell services like frequency regulation—turning parked cars into distributed power plants.
learn.c2_title: ⚡ Grid Services: Frequency Regulation & Peak Shaving
learn.c2_text: Aggregated EV fleets offer fast-reacting ancillary services. For instance, in California, Nuvve demonstrated a school bus providing 45 kW of grid support. V2G can defer costly grid upgrades and reduce reliance on peaker plants. However, frequent cycling may age batteries—though studies show minimal degradation with proper management algorithms.
learn.c3_title: 🇮🇳 India Explores V2G for Urban Stability
learn.c3_text: India’s first V2G pilot was launched in Delhi by the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and Tata Motors. Using converted electric buses, the project tested grid support during peak hours. With over 1.4 million EVs registered in 2023, scaling V2G could unlock 20–30 GW of flexible capacity nationwide by 2030.
